title: Add a 'compute' chunk option to route chunk evaluation to a registered executor
description:
This adds a new chunk option, `compute`, that lets a code chunk evaluate somewhere else — another R process, or another machine — instead of in the host session:

- `#| compute: gpu` routes the chunk to the executor registered with `options(compute.executor = ...)`, e.g. `mirai::register_render()`, on profile `"gpu"`.
- `#| compute: true` routes to the backend's default profile.
- Untagged chunks evaluate locally, exactly as before, including through a user-customized `evaluate` knit hook.

The `evaluate()` arguments are assembled once and shared by both paths. The worker half, `eng_r_remote()`, evaluates the chunk in the executing process's global environment, records plots on a fresh device, and returns the result together with the alt text collected by `record_fig_alt()` — so automatic `fig.alt` (e.g. `ggplot2::labs(alt = ...)`) works on routed chunks.

The new `?opts_chunk` section documents the option and the practical details.

Tests use a one-line mock executor and cover forwarding, `fig.alt`, custom `knit_print`, `log.echo`, caching, and validation. The integration test runs against mirai sync daemons, which evaluate in-process, so it stays CRAN-safe; it checks tagged-chunk output, host-saved figures (multiple, with non-default `fig.dim`), and that a routed `error: false` chunk aborts the render. `mirai` is added to Suggests for this test.

Risk is small: the option is never consulted for untagged chunks, and untagged documents render byte-identically to `master`.

@yihui @cderv this is along the lines of what we discussed. Comments / suggestions welcome!  (The corresponding mirai PR is https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/pull/655).

title: Let `fig.sep` override the blank line between captioned figures
description:
Since 1.52, `hook_plot_md_base()` and `hook_plot_md_pandoc()` append a blank line after each captioned figure except the last, so Pandoc emits a figure per image. Two changes:

- The blank line is only added when `fig.cap` is set explicitly. Plain `knit()` has a default caption (`plot of chunk <label>`) that previously triggered it, which broke inline images.
- The chunk option `fig.sep` can override the blank line; `fig.sep = ''` restores the old single-paragraph output.

Draft until the reporter confirms this matches what they need.

Closes #2529

title: Fix invalid LaTeX when warning/message/error is the only chunk output
description:
When a chunk produces only a warning (or message/error) with no text output, the generated `\begin{kframe}` environment contains leading blank lines, causing LaTeX to error with `"Something's wrong--perhaps a missing \item"`.

**Root cause:** `.color.block()` (backing the warning/message/error hooks) always prepends `\n\n` to create paragraph separation from preceding content. When there is no preceding content, these blank lines land at the very start of the `kframe` environment, which the `framed` package cannot handle.

**Fix:** Strip leading newlines from the assembled chunk content before wrapping in `\begin{kframe}`:

```r
# R/hooks-latex.R — .chunk.hook.tex()
# Before
x = .rm.empty.envir(paste0(k1, x, k2))
# After
x = .rm.empty.envir(paste0(k1, sub('^\n+', '', x), k2))
```

This is safe: source output never starts with `\n`, and the `\n\n` separator between source and a trailing warning is preserved (it is not at the head of `x`). The stripping only fires when warning/message/error is the first content in the frame.

**Test:** Added assertion to `test-hooks-latex.R` verifying that a warning-only chunk produces no leading blank lines inside `\begin{kframe}`.

title: Fix knit_exit() leaving knitr in non-functioning state for subsequent knit() calls
description:
After `knit_exit()` is called in the last (or only) chunk of a document, `.knitEnv$terminate` remains set, causing all subsequent `knit()` calls to immediately exit and produce empty output.

**Root cause:** The `terminate` check in `process_file()` sits at the *start* of each loop iteration. When `knit_exit()` is called in the final chunk, the loop ends with no further iterations — the cleanup path (`knit_exit(NULL, NULL)`) is never reached and the flag persists across calls.

```r
knitr::knit("knit_exit.Rmd")  # sets .knitEnv$terminate, never cleared
knitr::knit("hello.Rmd")      # sees stale terminate flag, exits immediately → empty output
```

## Changes

- **`R/output.R`**: Reset `.knitEnv$terminate = NULL` at the start of each top-level (non-child) `knit()` call, ensuring stale exit state never bleeds into a subsequent session.
- **`tests/testit/test-output.R`**: Regression test verifying that a `knit()` following a `knit_exit()` produces correct output.

title: Detect the tangle language in Typst documents too
description:
`detect_tangle_lang()` (from #2503 and 3376727d) returns early unless `out_format('markdown')`, on the reasoning that only markdown chunk headers carry the engine name. Typst headers carry it the same way (`{engine ...}`, `R/pattern.R`), and `parse_only()` already groups them, `md = type %in% c('md', 'typst')`. So on current master:

```r
writeLines(c("```{python}", "x = 1", "```"), "b.Rtyp"); purl("b.Rtyp")   # "b.R", Python commented out
writeLines(c("```{python}", "x = 1", "```"), "c.Rmd");  purl("c.Rmd")    # "c.py"
```

This widens the guard to `c('markdown', 'typst')` and updates its comment. The feature is not released yet, so I did not add a NEWS item; the existing 1.53 entry for #1928 already describes the intended behaviour.

title: feat(engine): add Rust engine
description:
This PR adds a Rust engine to knitr using extendr.

The engine should behave more or less like the Rcpp engine. It does one of two things. 
1. If `rust.source = FALSE`, it dispatches to `rextendr::eng_extendr()`, which compiles the Rust code to a single R function, evaluates it in R, and returns the result of the last line.
2. If `rust.source = TRUE`, it dispatches to `rextendr::eng_extendrsrc()`, which compiles the Rust code and makes Rust functions and structs annotated with `#[extendr]` macro available to call in other R code chunks. 

I also added a test and put `rextendr` in suggests. Additional information for the underlying engines can be found in the rextendr documentation:

```r
library(rextendr)
help("eng_extendr")
```

and at [extendr.rs](https://extendr.rs/).

And while I'm here, wanted to say thank you for all the work you've put into supporting the R community all these years!

Closes #2523.

title: Add Typst (.Rtyp) input format support
description:
knitr had no support for Typst documents — users couldn't embed and execute R code chunks in `.typ` files and get Typst-native output (especially figures) back.

## New: `.Rtyp` format

Input `.Rtyp` → knitted `.typ` → compiled `.pdf` via `typst compile`.

Chunk syntax reuses the backtick-fence style (also valid in Typst):

````typst
#set page(margin: 2cm)

= My Document

```{r plot, out.width="80%"}
plot(1:10)
```

The mean is `r mean(1:10)`.
````

Produces valid Typst output:

```typst
#figure(
  image("figure/plot-1.pdf", width: 80%),
  caption: [plot of chunk plot],
)
```

## Changes

- **`R/hooks-typst.R`** *(new)*: `hooks_typst()`, `render_typst()`, `hook_plot_typst()` — source/output/warning/message/error in raw ` ``` ``` ` blocks; plots via `#image()` / `#figure(image(), caption: [...])`
- **`R/pattern.R`**: adds `typst` entry to `all_patterns` (backtick-fence, same as `md`); `rtyp` extension detection in `detect_pattern()`; `pat_typst()` convenience function
- **`R/output.R`**: `rtyp` → `typst` in format switch and `ext2fmt`; `.Rtyp` → `.typ` in `auto_out_name()`
- **`R/utils-conversion.R`**: Typst compilation inlined into `knit2pdf()`; `knit2pdf()` auto-detects the `typst` compiler when output is `.typ` and accepts `compiler = 'typst'`
- **`R/utils.R`**: `typst` case in `format_sci_one()` — scientific notation renders as `$1.5 times 10^4$`
- **`NAMESPACE` / `DESCRIPTION`**: exports `pat_typst`, `render_typst`, `hooks_typst`, `hook_plot_typst`; adds `hooks-typst.R` to `Collate`
- **`NEWS.md`**: new feature entry under v1.52
- **`man/`**: updated Rd files (`hook_plot.Rd`, `output_hooks.Rd`, `pat_fun.Rd`, `knit2pdf.Rd`) via `roxygen2::roxygenize()`

title: Support custom cache pack/unpack via S3 generics for non-serializable objects
description:
This PR allows implementing `knit_cache_hook` methods which may preprocess objects (e.g., save to an external file) and define custom loaders.

I will add a NEWS item after we agree with the design.

- refactor(cache): use saveRDS/readRDS instead of makeLazyLoadDB/lazyload
    - For migration, `cache_save` replaces rdb/rdx files with rds file
    - For backward compatibility, `cache_load()` attempts `lazyload()` if rdb/rdx files are available
- ~~feat(cache): allow pre/postprocessing cache objects)~~
    - `knit_cache_preprocess` preprocesses objects being saved
    - `knit_cache_postprocess` postprocesses objects being loaded 
- feat!(cache): implement knit_cache_hook instead of pre/post-processors
    - Call `knit_cache_hook` methods on saving cache
        - Methods may save extra files under `${cache_path(h)}__extra` directory
        - Methods may return custom loader functions which is saved to `${cache_path(h).rds}`

With this PR, we can add some hooks on objects to be cached.
For example, we can use writeLines to save character objects.

````
```{r}
library(knitr)
registerS3method(
  "knit_cache_hook",
  "character",
  function(x, nm, path) {
    # Cache x as is if it extends character class
    if (!identical(class(x), "character")) {
      return(x)
    }

    # Preprocess data (e.g., save data to an external file)
    # Create external files under the directory of `paste0(path, "__extra")`
    # if knitr should cleanup them on refreshing/cleaning cache
    d <- paste0(path, "__extra")
    dir.create(d, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
    f <- file.path(d, paste0(nm, '.txt'))
    writeLines(x, f)

    # Return loader function
    # which receives ellipsis for future extentions and has knit_cache_loader class
    structure(function(...) readLines(f), class = 'knit_cache_loader')
  },
  envir = asNamespace("knitr")
)
```

```{r, cache=TRUE}
x <- 'foo bar'
print(x)
```

```{r}
print(x)
```
````

title: Use knitr-examples' composite action to install example dependencies
description:
The `Check knitr examples` workflow hardcoded the example dependencies (R packages read from a plain-text file, apt packages, CTAN packages) that logically belong to the **knitr-examples** repository. That duplicated maintenance across two repos.

knitr-examples now ships a composite action (`.github/actions/setup`) that installs everything needed to knit and compile the examples:

- R packages from its `DESCRIPTION` (`Suggests`), via `yihui/actions/setup-r-dependencies` (which **caches** them across runs)
- system/apt packages
- LaTeX setup (`tinytex::r_texmf("add")` + `dvisvgm`; other CTAN packages are auto-installed by `tinytex::latexmk()`)

This PR replaces the three hardcoded steps with a single call to that action (from the checked-out `knitr-examples` subdirectory). The dependency lists now live in one place.

`extra-packages` is left empty here so the development version of knitr installed earlier in this workflow is **not** clobbered.

Companion change: yihui/knitr-examples@6be97c7 (adds the action; the examples repo's own site build reuses it).

title: Stash the raw chunk body as `original.code` for Quarto (#2239)
description:
The last open item of #2239: under `echo: fenced`, Quarto echoes the original
chunk content, but when the `code` or `file` chunk option supplies the body,
`get_code()` swaps in the replacement before the source hook runs, so the
fenced echo showed the replacement rather than what was written in the document.

This stashes the raw body partition (`parts$code`, before any `code`/`file`
substitution) as `original.code` in the `quarto_options` bundle, so Quarto can
retrieve the original content in its `echo: fenced` option hook.

@cderv confirmed both the partition (`parts$code`) and the field name
(`original.code`) work for the Quarto side.

Closes #2239

title: Don't duplicate class.source as language for cat chunks
description:
Closes #2519

A `cat` chunk that sets its language via `class.source` (e.g. ` ```{cat, class.source='sh'} `) emitted that class twice in the output fence (` ```{.sh .sh} `).

`eng_cat()` passed `class.source` to `set_lang()` as the default language, which copied it to `options$lang` but left `class.source` set, so the markdown source hook appended it a second time next to the resolved `lang`.

The conflation is specific to `cat`: it is the only engine that feeds `class.source` in as the default language. The other `set_lang()` callers (`eng_interpreted`, `eng_embed`) derive the default from the engine name or file extension, where `class.source` is a genuinely additive extra class. So the fix stays in `eng_cat` rather than being generalized into `set_lang()`.

Now `class.source` is promoted to the language and cleared when it is the sole source of the language, so it is emitted only once. Using `lang` and `class.source` together still adds the extra class.

| header | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `` ```{cat, class.source='sh'} `` | `` ```{.sh .sh} `` | `` ``` sh `` |
| `` ```{cat, lang='sh'} `` | `` ``` sh `` | `` ``` sh `` |
| `` ```{cat, lang='sh', class.source='extra'} `` | `` ```{.sh .extra} `` | `` ```{.sh .extra} `` |

Added a regression test in `test-engine.R`.

title: Make the "Quitting from" file path a clickable link
description:
Closes #2153.

When a chunk errors out, knitr prints a message like:

```
Quitting from file.Rmd:492-501 [chunk-label]
```

This wraps the file path in an [OSC 8 terminal hyperlink](https://gist.github.com/egmontkob/eb114294efbcd5adb1944c9f3cb5feda) that points to the first failing line, so a front-end that supports terminal hyperlinks can make the path clickable and jump straight to the error location. This is the original request: one click to reach the error.

## Approach

No new dependency — the same technique already used in [litedown](https://github.com/yihui/litedown). The link is emitted only when the front-end advertises support (the RStudio IDE sets `RSTUDIO_CLI_HYPERLINKS=true`); otherwise the plain path is printed exactly as before, so there is no risk of stray escape sequences in environments that don't render them. The "Quitting from" message goes to `stderr` as a diagnostic and never enters the rendered document.

```r
ansi_path = function(file, lines = '') {
  if (!length(file) || is.na(file) || file == '') return(file)
  if (!isTRUE(as.logical(Sys.getenv('RSTUDIO_CLI_HYPERLINKS')))) return(file)
  line = as.integer(strsplit(lines, '-', fixed = TRUE)[[1]][1])
  if (is.na(line)) return(file)
  sprintf(
    '\033]8;line = %d:col = 1;file://%s\a%s\033]8;;\a',
    line, normalizePath(file, mustWork = FALSE), file
  )
}
```

Regression test added in `test-output.R` (no link without support; OSC 8 link with `line`/`col` params when supported).

title: Show rlang backtraces for warnings, not just errors
description:
Closes #2219.

The issue asked for two things: move rlang's error-traceback hook into knitr, and do the same for warnings.

The error side already landed via #2388 — knitr installs `rlang::entrace()` as an error calling handler, so errors during knitting get a backtrace. This PR adds the warning half, which was blocked in 2023 because the relevant rlang tools were private. rlang has since made warning tracing public (`entrace()` handles warnings, and `conditionMessage.rlang_warning()` renders the trace), so knitr can own it now.

## Change

A single gated calling handler in `.onLoad()`:

```r
warning = function(w) {
  opt = getOption('rlang_backtrace_on_warning_report')
  if (!is.null(opt) && !identical(opt, 'none')) rlang::entrace(w)
}
```

`entrace()` turns the warning into an `rlang_warning` whose `conditionMessage()` includes the backtrace, so the existing `sew.warning()` displays it with no change. (An earlier version also appended the trace in `sew.warning()`, which double-printed it — letting rlang format the message is the correct, simpler approach.)

## Opt-in

Off by default. Enable with the same option rlang consults at the top level:

```r
options(rlang_backtrace_on_warning_report = "full")   # or "branch"
```

Gating at the handler means no backtrace is computed for the common case, and the warning condition is left untouched when the feature is off.

## Result

````
```{r}
f <- function() g()
g <- function() warning("oops")
f()
```
````

```
## Warning in g(): oops
## Backtrace:
##     ▆
##  1. └─global f()
##  2.   └─global g()
```

Regression test added in `test-block.R` (off → no backtrace; `full` → backtrace shown exactly once).

title: Don't parse SQL chunks without ?-placeholders for interpolation
description:
Closes rstudio/rmarkdown#2342.

## Problem

A `sql` chunk whose query contains a string literal with an apostrophe (and no `?`-style interpolation variable) fails to render. The reported case is a Postgres [dollar-quoted string constant](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-SYNTAX-CONSTANTS):

````
```{sql, connection=mydb}
SELECT $$Dianne's horse$$;
```
````

```
Error in sqlParseVariablesImpl(sql, list(sqlQuoteSpec("\"", "\""), sqlQuoteSpec("'", ...
  Unterminated literal
```

## Cause

`eng_sql()` always calls `DBI::sqlParseVariables()` (and later `DBI::sqlInterpolate()`) to discover `?`-style interpolation variables — even when the query has no `?` placeholder at all. Those functions re-lex the SQL with a fixed set of quote specs (`"` and `'`) and don't understand dollar-quoting, so the `'` inside `Dianne's` is read as an unterminated literal. The query is valid; knitr had no reason to parse it in the first place.

## Fix

- `varnames_from_sql()`: skip `DBI::sqlParseVariables()` when the query contains no `?`.
- `interpolate_from_env()`: return the query verbatim when there are no interpolation variables (so `sqlInterpolate()`, which also re-lexes, is not called).

Interpolation of `?`-variables is unchanged and covered by a new regression test in `test-sql.R`.

title: Echo non-evaluated lines without a comment mask when eval is numeric
description:
Closes #2129.

When the chunk option `eval` is a numeric vector, only the selected lines are evaluated. To make `evaluate()` skip the other lines while still echoing them, knitr comments them out — but it used the `## ` prefix, which then leaked into the echoed source:

````
```{r, eval=2}
mtcars
1 + 41
```
````

previously echoed

``` r
## mtcars
1 + 41
```

so the non-evaluated line could not be shown as real code. This was the blocker in the reporter's use case (show `mtcars`, but only run `rmarkdown::paged_table(mtcars)`).

This masks the non-evaluated lines with a sentinel comment (`#<knitr>`) instead, and strips the sentinel from the echoed source after evaluation, following @yihui's suggestion in the thread. The same chunk now echoes both lines verbatim and runs only the second:

``` r
mtcars
1 + 41
```

### Notes

- Combines with `echo` as expected: `echo=1, eval=2` shows only line 1's source but runs only line 2.
- A real comment on a masked line is preserved (only the sentinel is removed).
- Multi-line masked expressions are handled (the sentinel is stripped from continuation lines too).
- No cache impact: the cache hash is built from the original chunk code, not the masked copy, and the cached output list is captured after stripping.

Includes a test and a NEWS entry.

title: Add chunk option log.echo to stream executing code to stderr
description:
Closes #2222.

When rendering in remote or batch contexts, it can be hard to tell which code is running (or which line is slow, or where an error came from) before the output document is produced. `evaluate::evaluate()` gained a `log_echo` argument (r-lib/evaluate#118) that logs each expression to `stderr` immediately before it runs. This exposes it as a chunk option.

Set `log.echo=TRUE` on a chunk (or `knitr::opts_chunk$set(log.echo = TRUE)` document-wide) and each expression is echoed to `stderr` as it executes:

````
```{r log.echo=TRUE}
x <- 1
slow_thing()
x + 1
```
````

Most logging platforms add a timestamp to each `stderr` line, so this also shows which code is taking a long time.

### Notes

- **No `opts_chunk` default.** `log.echo` is deliberately *not* added to the `opts_chunk` defaults: introducing a new default option would change every chunk's cache hash and invalidate all existing caches. Left unset, `options$log.echo` is `NULL` and `isTRUE()` treats it as `FALSE`, so behavior is unchanged unless the user opts in.
- **Dependency bump.** `log_echo` requires `evaluate >= 1.0.0`; `DESCRIPTION` is bumped accordingly (current CRAN evaluate is 1.0.5).
- Scoped to code echoing only; `evaluate`'s companion `log_warning` is left for a separate request if wanted.

Includes a test and a NEWS entry.

title: spin(): add roxygen argument to preserve roxygen2 blocks as code
description:
Closes #2317.

By default, `spin()` converts every `#'` line to documentation prose. That mangles **roxygen2** comments — a script with `#' @param` / `#' @export` above a function loses those tags when spun.

This adds an opt-in `roxygen` argument. When `roxygen = TRUE`, a block of consecutive `#'` lines that contains a roxygen tag (a line like `#' @param`) is kept **verbatim** inside the code chunk instead of being stripped to prose, so the spun document is still valid **roxygen2** input. A `#'` block without any tag is still treated as documentation, so plain prose keeps working.

Using the reporter's example:

```r
text = c(
  "#' Say hello to a user",
  "#' @param name The person who you are greeting",
  "#' @export",
  "say_hello <- function(name = '') print(paste0('Hello ', name))"
)
spin(text = text, format = "qmd", knit = FALSE, roxygen = TRUE)
```

    ```{r}
    #' Say hello to a user
    #' @param name The person who you are greeting
    #' @export
    say_hello <- function(name = '') print(paste0('Hello ', name))
    ```

The default (`roxygen = FALSE`) is unchanged. Detection is the reporter's heuristic (a block is roxygen iff it contains an `@tag` line) — simple and imperfect by design, but avoids a **roxygen2** dependency (which would be circular, as roxygen2 imports knitr).

Includes a test and a NEWS entry.

title: Verbatim chunks ignore a global echo = FALSE (#2239)
description:
Addresses the first checklist item of #2239 (leaving the rest of the list open).

A `verbatim` chunk exists to display its content, so an inherited global `echo = FALSE` should not silence it. This is a real trip-hazard when a format sets `echo: false` as a default — Quarto's `revealjs` does — because a `{verbatim}` chunk then outputs nothing unless the author remembers to add `echo: true` to it.

**Behavior:**
- A global `echo = FALSE` (inherited from `opts_chunk$set()` / a format default) is ignored by `verbatim`/`embed` — the content is shown.
- An `echo` set on the chunk itself is still honored, so `echo = FALSE` on a specific `verbatim` chunk keeps hiding it. This answers the open question in the thread about how a user would deliberately hide a verbatim chunk.

The two cases are told apart with a small helper `chunk_option()` that reads an option as written in the chunk header (before it is merged with the global options). This works for both the classic header syntax (`{verbatim, echo=FALSE}`) and the `#|` cell-option syntax.

Verified with a new test in `test-engine.R` covering all three paths.

title: Add optional internal debug logging via debugme (#2203)
description:
Closes #2203.

Wires up [debugme](https://cran.r-project.org/package=debugme) for debugging knitr and packages that build on it, following the design agreed in the issue thread.

**Strictly opt-in.** `.onLoad()` only activates it when the `DEBUGME` environment variable is set to include `knitr` and debugme is installed:

```r
if (Sys.getenv('DEBUGME') != '' && requireNamespace('debugme', quietly = TRUE))
  debugme::debugme()
```

So the feature has zero effect — and debugme is never even loaded — unless a developer explicitly turns it on (e.g. `Sys.setenv(DEBUGME = "knitr")` before `library(knitr)`). debugme is added to `Suggests`.

**Markers.** A few `!DEBUG` string-literal markers are seeded at natural points in the chunk pipeline (chunk execution entry, cache load, cache save). debugme rewrites these literals into log calls at load time; when logging is disabled they are inert no-op statements. More can be added over time.

Verified end-to-end: with `DEBUGME=knitr`, knitting a cached chunk logs `block_exec()` + `saving cache` on the first run and `loading cache` on a re-run; with `DEBUGME` unset, output is silent. Existing block/cache/engine tests pass.

title: Add quarto_profile() to read/check the active Quarto profile (#2216)
description:
Closes #2216.

Adds `quarto_profile()`, a small helper mirroring `pandoc_to()`:

- `quarto_profile()` returns the active Quarto profile name(s) read from the `QUARTO_PROFILE` environment variable (comma-separated when multiple profiles are active; surrounding whitespace is trimmed), or an empty character vector when no profile is active.
- `quarto_profile("production")` returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` for whether any of the given names is active.

This makes profile-conditional chunk output concise, e.g. `eval = knitr::quarto_profile("production")`, instead of `Sys.getenv("QUARTO_PROFILE") == "production"` (which also mishandles the multi-profile case).

title: include_url(): honor the chunk option out.height for the iframe (#1998)
description:
Addresses the `out.height` part of #1998.

`sew.knit_embed_url()` (the `sew()` method behind `include_url()` / `include_app()`) already honored `out.width` for the iframe width, but ignored `out.height` — it always used the `height` passed to `include_url()` (default `400px`). @cderv noted the asymmetry: you had to set the height on the function call rather than via the chunk option.

This makes the height honor `out.height`, falling back to `include_url()`'s `height` argument when `out.height` is unset, mirroring how `out.width` works:

```r
options$out.height %n% x$height %n% "400px"
```

Behavior:

| chunk option | `include_url(height=)` | iframe height |
|---|---|---|
| — | (default `400px`) | `400px` (unchanged) |
| — | `800px` | `800px` (unchanged) |
| `out.height="600px"` | (default) | `600px` |
| `out.height="200px"` | `800px` | `200px` (chunk option wins) |

The other two ideas in #1998 are intentionally not included here:

- **`attr.output` as an alias for `out.extra`**: these target different things (`attr.output` decorates the output *block*; `out.extra` adds attributes *inside* the tag), so aliasing them would be confusing. `out.extra` remains the way to add iframe attributes.
- **named-vector `out.extra`**: low value over the existing `out.extra = c("data-external=1", ...)` form (as noted on the issue).

## Tests

Added a test in `test-plot.R` calling `sew()` on an `include_url()` object directly (no network/screenshot), asserting `out.height` wins, the `include_url()` height is used otherwise, and `out.width` still applies.

title: Add vignette_depends() to skip evaluation when \VignetteDepends are unmet (#2164)
description:
Closes #2164.

Implements the helper @yihui sketched on the issue.

A vignette often illustrates a package in combination with others that are only in `Suggests` and may be unavailable when the vignette is built (e.g. on CRAN). Today the author has to guard evaluation by hand, e.g.:

```r
required <- c("B", "C", "D")
if (!all(sapply(required, requireNamespace, quietly = TRUE)))
  knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

If those packages are already declared via `\VignetteDepends{B, C, D}`, this is redundant. `vignette_depends()` reads that declaration from the current input (`current_input()` + `tools::vignetteInfo()`), and sets `eval = FALSE` for the rest of the vignette when any declared package is missing:

```r
# first code chunk of the vignette
knitr::vignette_depends()
```

The missing packages are returned invisibly, so the author can also message about them if desired. Chunks are still *shown*; only evaluation is turned off. When all dependencies are present, nothing changes.

## Tests

Added a test in `test-utils.R` that builds a small vignette twice — once with a `\VignetteDepends{}` naming a non-existent package (later chunk is skipped) and once with installed packages (later chunk runs).

title: hook_purl(): preserve `#|` cell options in the tangled script (#2414)
description:
Closes #2414.

Since #2268, `purl()` preserves the `#|` cell options in its output. But `hook_purl()` — the hook that writes the tangled script *while weaving* a document (`knit_hooks$set(purl = hook_purl)`) — still dropped them:

````
```{r}
#| eval: false
#| fig.width: 8
1 + 1
```
````

Tangled via `hook_purl()`, this produced just:

```r
## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1 + 1
```

The reason (as @yihui noted on the issue) is that the `#|` lines live in the parsed block's `params.chunk`, reachable from `tangle_block()` but not from `hook_purl()`, which only receives the merged chunk options.

## Fix

Stash the raw `#|` option lines as a `chunk_src` attribute on `knit_code`, right next to the existing `chunk_opts` attribute (the same channel that already carries per-chunk data). `hook_purl()` then reads it and passes it to `label_code()` via `params.chunk`, so its output matches `purl()`:

```r
## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#| eval: false
#| fig.width: 8
# 1 + 1
```

Chunks without `#|` options are unaffected (`chunk_src` is `NULL`).

## Tests

Added a test in `test-tangle.R` that weaves a real document with `hook_purl()` set and asserts the `#|` lines appear in the tangled script.

title: Rcpp engine: compile from files so a source can #include sibling headers (#2367)
description:
Closes #2367.

An `Rcpp` chunk that reads code from files via the `file` option previously compiled the *concatenated* content of those files. A source file containing `#include "foo.h"` then failed to compile, because `Rcpp::sourceCpp()` builds in a temporary directory where the sibling header does not exist. This is also why the `file = c("foo.h", "foo.cpp")` suggestion did not work.

## Fix

When the `file` option is set, `eng_Rcpp()` now compiles the file(s) directly instead of the concatenated code:

- all listed files are copied into one build directory under their original basenames;
- the last `.cpp`/`.cc`/`.cxx` file is compiled with `sourceCpp(file = ...)`.

Because `sourceCpp()` adds the source file's directory to the include path, a source file can now `#include` its sibling headers. This covers both cases from the issue:

````md
```{Rcpp, file=c("foo.h", "foo.cpp")}
```
````

Inline Rcpp chunks (no `file` option) are unchanged — the hot path still calls `sourceCpp(code = ...)`.

## Tests

Added a test in `test-engine.R`. It first probes that a trivial inline `Rcpp` chunk compiles (Rcpp can load without a C++ toolchain, e.g. on some CRAN machines), and skips only if that probe fails. The actual assertion — a chunk with `file = c("inc.h", "src.cpp")` compiles and its exported function works — then runs unguarded, so a regression in the multi-file path surfaces as a failure rather than being masked as a skip.

title: Add a ps engine for PowerShell (#1932)
description:
Closes #1932.

Adds a `ps` engine that runs PowerShell code chunks:

- The chunk is written to a `.ps1` script and executed with `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File`. PowerShell requires the `.ps1` extension and the `-File` argument (as found by @cderv in the issue); `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` lets the unsigned temp script run under Windows' default execution policy.
- It is a thin wrapper around the generic `exec` engine, so the command is overridable via `engine.opts`, e.g. `engine.opts = list(command = "pwsh")` to use the newer cross-platform PowerShell.
- Code is highlighted as `powershell`.

The test runs PowerShell only when it is both found and verified executable (a trivial probe command must succeed first), so it is skipped on machines without a working PowerShell (e.g. CRAN/Linux) rather than failing.

title: purl(): tangle documents whose first chunk is a non-R language (#1928)
description:
Closes #1928.

When the first code chunk of a document is not R but another language, `purl()` tangles the document to a script in that language instead of an `.R` script:

- The output file uses the engine name as its extension by default, with a few overrides (e.g. `python` → `.py`, `ruby` → `.rb`). Pass the `output` argument to override.
- Chunks of that language are kept as-is (runnable); chunks of any other language are ignored.
- Chunk headers become `#%%` code cells, using the language's comment character from xfun's `comment_chars` (block comments such as C's `/* */` are closed).
- R-first documents are unaffected (still tangle to R, other-language chunks commented out as before).

The target language is decided by the first code chunk, per the design discussion in the issue, which keeps detection simple and sidesteps the child-document language-detection problem.

title: Add chunk option fig.cap.command to customize the LaTeX figure caption command (#1872)
description:
Closes #1872.

## Problem

The figure caption command in `hook_plot_tex()` is hard-coded as `\caption`. Some LaTeX document classes need a different command for certain figures — e.g. AMS journals use `\appendcaption` for figures in an appendix. Until now the only workaround was to copy and rewrite the entire plot hook.

## Fix

New chunk option `fig.cap.command` overrides the caption command. It defaults to `\caption`, so existing behavior is unchanged:

````
```{r fig.cap="An appendix figure.", fig.cap.command="\\appendcaption", fig.scap=NA}
plot(1)
```
````

produces `\appendcaption{An appendix figure.}` instead of `\caption{...}`.

Notes:
- The option is intentionally **not** added to the default chunk options, to avoid invalidating the cache of existing documents. The hook falls back to `\caption` when it is unset.
- Commands like `\appendcaption` do not take the `[short caption]` optional argument, so set `fig.scap = NA` to suppress the auto-generated short caption when needed (shown above).

Test added in `tests/testit/test-hooks-latex.R`; full suite passes.

title: kable(): multiline table for `simple` format when cells contain line breaks (#2021)
description:
Closes #2021.

## Problem

Pandoc's simple tables cannot represent line breaks within a cell. A cell containing `\n` broke the layout — the extra lines leaked out as separate, misaligned rows:

```r
kable(data.frame(id = 1:2, text = c("line1\nline2", "bbbb")), format = "simple")
```

```
 id  text
---  ------
  1  line1
line2
  2  bbbb
```

## Fix

When any cell contains a line break, `kable(format = "simple")` now emits a Pandoc [multiline table](https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#extension-multiline_tables) instead. Cells are split into physical lines, logical rows are separated by a blank line, and the table is delimited by rules at the top and bottom:

```
---  ------
 id  text
---  ------
  1  line1
     line2

  2  bbbb
---  ------
```

The headerless case uses a top rule in place of the header row. Tables without any line breaks are unchanged. I verified the generated source round-trips through Pandoc as a proper multiline table (header, body, caption, and alignment all parsed correctly).

This is the behavior approved in the issue thread ("it will be nice to switch to a multiline table when \n is detected in the table cells").

Snapshot tests added in `tests/testit/test-table.md`; full test suite passes.

title: kable(): accessibility scope attributes in HTML tables (#1747)
description:
Closes #1747

Adds accessibility markup to the HTML tables generated by `kable()`, per the [WAI tables tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/).

- **`scope="col"` on column headers** — emitted unconditionally. It lets screen readers associate each data cell with its column header, and does not change how the table renders.
- **`<th scope="row">` on row-name cells** — opt-in via `options(knitr.table.html.row.header = TRUE)`. When on, the first column (the row names) is marked up as row headers instead of `<td>`. Kept off by default because `<th>` may be styled differently from `<td>` (e.g., bold) and could affect existing CSS, so this does not silently change anyone's current output.

The empty corner cell above the row names is a header for neither dimension, so it gets no `scope`.

Snapshot tests in `test-table.md` cover both the default (`scope="col"` only) and the opt-in (`<th scope="row">`) output.

title: Add pkg_bib_nocite() for a nocite package bibliography (#1733)
description:
Closes #1733

`write_bib()` generates BibTeX entries for R packages but does not surface their citation keys. To list packages in the References section via the YAML `nocite` field (without citing them inline), users had to track the auto-generated keys by hand.

`pkg_bib_nocite()` returns those keys formatted for `nocite`, e.g. `@R-knitr, @R-xfun`. It captures **all** entries a package provides — not only the auto-generated `R-<pkg>` `Manual` entry, but also any extra preferred citations shipped in the package's `CITATION` (which carry their own keys).

Typical use in the YAML metadata:

```yaml
---
bibliography: packages.bib
nocite: '`r knitr::pkg_bib_nocite(c("knitr", "rmarkdown"), file = "packages.bib")`'
---
```

When `file = ''` (the default), the entries are discarded and only the keys are returned; the console echo that `xfun::pkg_bib()` produces for `file = ''` is suppressed so nothing leaks into the rendered output.

title: include_graphics(): add copy argument to copy images into the figure dir (#1513)
description:
Closes #1513.

Adds a `copy` argument to `include_graphics()`. When `copy = TRUE`, each image is copied into the current chunk's figure directory (named like the chunk's plots, e.g. `figure/label-1.png`) and the copy is included instead of the original.

This solves the case raised in the issue: a `magick`-image `knit_print` method (or any code) produces an image in `tempdir()`, which only works if pandoc embeds images. With `copy = TRUE` the file lands in the figure dir and survives to the rendering step of non-self-contained formats.

Default is off; the global default can be set via `options(knitr.graphics.copy = TRUE)`.

title: Allow a cached chunk to depend on an uncached chunk (#1039)
description:
Closes #1039

A cached chunk could previously only depend (via `dependson` or `autodep = TRUE`) on another **cached** chunk. The dependency was enforced by purging dependent chunks' caches whenever a dependency's cache was rebuilt — which cannot fire if the dependency has no cache. So the combination was rejected with the warning *"code chunks must not depend on the uncached chunk"*.

This changes the invalidation model from push to pull: instead of relying on a dependency firing a purge, the code of the chunks a cached chunk depends on (including transitive dependencies) is folded into its cache key. Changing a dependency's code then changes the dependent chunk's hash and invalidates the cache, regardless of whether the dependency is itself cached. The old purge mechanism is kept for `cache.rebuild`.

`dep_ancestors()` computes the transitive closure of a chunk's dependencies by inverting `dep_list` (which maps a chunk to its dependents). The now-unnecessary warning and its `warn.uncached.dep` flag are removed.

Tested: uncached dependency change invalidates the cached chunk; an unchanged dependency still yields a cache hit; transitive chains work; a chunk with no dependency is unaffected.

title: spin(): add engine argument for the default chunk engine (#1773)
description:
Adds an `engine` argument to `spin()` so a script written in another language can be spun into a report without setting `#+ engine=...` on every chunk.

```r
# a pure Python script: every chunk fence becomes ```{python}
spin('analysis.py')                  # engine guessed from the .py extension
spin('script.txt', engine = 'python')  # or set it explicitly
```

- The chunk fence carries the engine name, e.g. ` ```{python} ` (per @yihui's preference over `{r engine="python"}`).
- The default engine is guessed from the input file's extension (`.py` → `python`, `.jl` → `julia`, `.sh` → `bash`; everything else → `r`), and can be overridden via the `engine` argument.
- A chunk that sets its own `engine` option still overrides the fence at knit time.
- Only applies to the Markdown output formats (`Rmd`/`qmd`).

This addresses the follow-up request in the thread (spinning a fully non-R script); the original `#+ engine="python"` bug was already fixed in 74bcff8.

Closes #1773

title: Add label_chunks() to name unnamed code chunks (#2228)
description:
Closes #2228

Adds a new exported function `label_chunks()` that reads a document in knitr's Markdown chunk syntax, finds code chunks without a label, and inserts a generated label into each chunk header. Already-labeled chunks are left untouched.

```r
doc = c(
  "```{r}", "1 + 1", "```", "",
  "```{r, echo=FALSE}", "plot(cars)", "```", "",
  "```{r named}", "summary(cars)", "```"
)
cat(label_chunks(text = doc), sep = "\n")
#> ```{r unnamed-chunk-1}
#> 1 + 1
#> ```
#>
#> ```{r unnamed-chunk-2, echo=FALSE}
#> plot(cars)
#> ```
#>
#> ```{r named}
#> summary(cars)
#> ```
```

The label for each unnamed chunk is produced by a function passed via the `label` argument, called with the chunk's options and the index of the unnamed chunk, so labels can be derived from chunk options if desired. The default generates `prefix-i` labels (`prefix` defaults to the `unnamed.chunk.label` option, i.e. `unnamed-chunk`). Generated labels are made unique so they do not clash with labels already present in the document.

Signature mirrors `convert_chunk_header()`: `input`/`text` for the source, `output = NULL` returns the modified lines, a path or function (e.g. `output = identity`) writes back.

title: purl(): respect explicit comment option to comment out evaluated code (#1352)
description:
Closes #1352

Extends the `comment` chunk option (introduced for #2425) so it fully expresses the user's intention for whether tangled code is commented out, independent of `eval`:

- `comment` not set: `eval = FALSE` code is commented out with `#` (unchanged default); `eval = TRUE` code is kept uncommented.
- `comment` set explicitly: always respected. `comment = ""` (or `NA`) keeps code uncommented (#2425); a prefix like `comment = "#"` comments the code out even when `eval = TRUE` (#1352).

This lets users keep a record in the tangled R script of code that was run during knitting but should not be re-run from the script (e.g. a `knit_expand()` call), without resorting to a custom `hook_purl()`.

Both `purl()` (`tangle_block()`) and `knit(tangle = TRUE)` (`hook_purl()`) route through `tangle_mask()`, so both honor the option.

title: Run option hooks inside purl() so tangling can be driven by chunk options (#1903)
description:
Closes #1903.

Option hooks registered via `opts_hooks$set()` were only applied when knitting, not when tangling with `purl()` (`tangle_block()` never ran them). So a hook on `label` could not set `purl = FALSE`/`TRUE` to select which chunks get extracted — the user had to edit the source document to add `purl = FALSE` to unwanted chunks.

This factors the opts_hooks loop out of `call_block()` into a small `run_opts_hooks()` helper, and calls it in `tangle_block()` after chunk options are evaluated and before the `purl` check. Now a hook can drive tangling from other options, e.g. keep only chunks whose label matches a pattern:

```r
opts_hooks$set(label = function(options) {
  options$purl = grepl("-solution$|^setup$", options$label)
  options
})
```

NEWS and a test in `test-tangle.R` are added. Full testit suite passes.

title: Merge cache pack/unpack generics into a single process_cache() (#2340)
description:
Follow-up refactor of #2340. Having two S3 generics (`knit_cache_pack()` / `knit_cache_unpack()`) for the cache customization felt like too much surface for one feature. This collapses them into a single generic with a direction flag:

```r
process_cache(x, pack = TRUE, ...)
```

- `pack = TRUE` before an object is written to the cache (return a serializable version)
- `pack = FALSE` after an object is read from the cache (restore the original)

Dispatch is still on the object's class, so a packed object needs a different class from the original for the correct method to be found in each direction — exactly as before, and naturally satisfied by terra (`SpatRaster` ↔ `PackedSpatRaster`). Registration becomes:

```r
registerS3method(
  "process_cache", "SpatRaster",
  function(x, pack = TRUE, ...) if (pack) terra::wrap(x) else x,
  envir = asNamespace("knitr")
)
registerS3method(
  "process_cache", "PackedSpatRaster",
  function(x, pack = TRUE, ...) if (pack) x else terra::unwrap(x),
  envir = asNamespace("knitr")
)
```

Since #2340 has not been in a CRAN release yet, this is a safe API change with no deprecation needed. NEWS, docs, and tests updated accordingly.

@atusy heads-up on the new design — the pack/unpack pair from your PR is now a single `process_cache()` generic with a `pack` flag. Functionally equivalent; just a smaller API. Let me know if you see any issue.

title: purl(): let comment='' keep eval=FALSE code uncommented (#2425)
description:
Closes #2425.

When `purl()` tangles a chunk with `eval = FALSE`, its code is commented out in the R script (with `#`). This makes it impossible to produce a script in which such code is meant to be *run* — e.g. code that reads interactive input (which would hang during knitting, hence `eval = FALSE` in the source document) but should still execute when the script is run directly. `comment = ""` was tried by the reporter as a workaround but had no effect.

`tangle_mask()` now honors the chunk option `comment`: `comment = ""` (or `NA`) leaves the `eval = FALSE` code uncommented. The default behavior is unchanged (code is commented out with `#`).

Given a chunk `{r, eval=FALSE, comment=""}` containing `x <- 1`, `purl()` now emits the line uncommented (`x <- 1`); without `comment=""` it stays `# x <- 1` as before.

title: Use a plot object's own alt text (e.g. ggplot2::labs(alt=)) as the default fig.alt (#2001)
description: Fixes #2001. ## Problem Plot objects can carry their own alt text (e.g. `ggplot2::labs(alt = ...)`), but knitr had no way to use it as the default `fig.alt`. The only workaround was per-chunk boilerplate with `eval.after` + `!expr`: ```` ```{r} #| fig.alt: !expr last_alt p <- ggplot(...) + labs(alt = "...") last_alt <- ggplot2::get_alt_text(p) p ``` ```` ## This PR When `fig.alt` is not set, knitr reads the alt text stored in the plot object and uses it as the default. So this "just works": ```` ```{r} ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point() + labs(alt = "Scatterplot of mpg vs weight") ``` ```` → `` ## Design (revised — no public generic) An earlier revision of this PR introduced an exported S3 generic `fig_alt()` so any package could register a method. That was more machinery than the problem needs: **ggplot2** is the only plotting package today with a way to store alt text in the object, and knitr already recognizes special plot classes (`htmlwidget`, `shiny.tag`) by class in the same `evaluate` value handler. So this now: - recognizes alt-carrying plots by class (`.alt.classes`, currently just `ggplot`) in the value handler, right next to the existing `htmlwidget`/`shiny.tag` checks; - reads the text via `get_alt_text()` (fetched from the **ggplot2** namespace, available since ggplot2 3.4.0), collected in plot-printing order; - merges into `fig.alt` after chunk evaluation (alongside the `eval.after` pass), so nothing mutates a consumed option or unlocks `opts_current` mid-evaluation (#1798). No exported API, no `NAMESPACE`/man/`.onLoad` changes. A new plotting package can be supported later by extending `.alt.classes` and `plot_alt_text()`. ## Behavior - **Multi-plot chunks:** `fig.alt` is already a per-plot recyclable vector, so `collected[i]` maps to plot `i`. - **Precedence / mixing:** an explicit `fig.alt` wins element-wise; `NA` (or `""`) falls back to the plot's own alt text, so `fig.alt = c(NA, "custom")` works. - **Alignment safety:** only recognized plot classes occupy a slot (ordinary printed values don't shift the mapping); a recognized plot with no alt text gets an `NA` placeholder. - **Known limitation (unchanged):** base-graphics plots are side-effect recorded with no printed object, so in a chunk mixing base plots with ggplot objects the positional mapping could drift; homogeneous chunks (the common case) align exactly.

title: Let opts_hooks options take precedence over engine-modified options at the chunk hook (#2488)
description:
Closes #2488. Also unblocks quarto-dev/quarto-cli#14910.

## Problem

Follow-up to #2333/#2477. Since #2333, options that a language engine changes internally (e.g. the `css`/`js`/`sass`/`scss` engines set `results = 'asis'` so their raw HTML is written verbatim) are attached to the engine output and handed to the `chunk` hook, so it agrees with the `output` hook.

But that engine change reaches the `chunk` hook **unconditionally**, silently overriding any value an `opts_hooks` callback set for the same option earlier in the pipeline. @cderv found this breaks Quarto: `knitr_options_hook` forces `results = 'hold'` whenever it detects an inline annotation marker (e.g. a trailing `/* <1> */` in a `css` chunk), specifically so Quarto's own `chunk` hook decides how to wrap the output. Once knitr picked up #2333 on the dev channel, that override stopped taking effect for `css`/`scss`/`sass` chunks and the annotation markup silently disappeared.

## Approach

The first commit special-cased the four built-in engines. That only patched the built-ins and left the same hole open for any third-party engine, so this PR replaces it with a single, general rule (see the diff — the earlier commit's `engine_output()` `chunk_opts` argument and per-engine changes are reverted):

- In `block.R`, record which options an `opts_hooks` callback actually changed.
- After the engine runs, when recovering the engine-modified options for the `chunk` hook (#2333), re-apply the `opts_hooks`-changed options on top.

So an option set by `opts_hooks` is the user's final word and wins over an engine's later internal change, regardless of which engine is used. The #2333 behavior is otherwise unchanged: an engine's change still flows to the `chunk` hook for any option `opts_hooks` did not touch.

## Verification

- @cderv's reproducer: on master the `.wrapped` div silently disappears; with this change it is restored, and the `<style>` block is still written verbatim.
- New regression test in `tests/testit/test-engine.R` using a plain `demo` engine (not one of the four built-ins), asserting the `opts_hooks` value reaches the `chunk` hook even though the engine forces `results = 'asis'`. The existing #2333 test still passes.

title: read_chunk(): read chunks from a knitr document by label (#2041)
description:
Closes #2041.

## Motivation

`read_chunk()` currently only understands **R scripts**, where chunks are delimited by `## ---- label ----` markers. #2041 (from @cderv) asks for it to also read a **knitr source document** (e.g. `.Rmd`, `.Rnw`) and pick up its code chunks by chunk label, so they can be reused elsewhere — mirroring the community request it links to.

## What this does

When `read_chunk()` is given a document rather than an R script, it extracts the code chunks and registers them keyed by chunk label, so a later chunk referencing that label reuses the code (the same mechanism as chunks read from an R script — code is stored unevaluated).

```r
# ext-src.Rmd contains:
#   ```{r ext-chunk}
#   z <- 99
#   ```

knitr::read_chunk("ext-src.Rmd")
```

````
```{r ext-chunk}
```
value is `r z`   # -> value is 99
````

## Design

- **Detection** — the document type is resolved from the file extension via `detect_pattern()`, or from the content when reading from `lines=` without a path. If the input isn't a recognized knitr document, `read_chunk()` falls back to the existing R-script parsing. R-script behavior is unchanged, and is also always used when `labels=` is supplied.
- **Extraction** — a lightweight `chunks_from_doc()` reuses the existing `divide_chunks()` / pattern machinery to split chunks and reads the label from the chunk header (`xfun::csv_options()`), rather than going through the much heavier `parse_block()` (which merges options, tracks dependencies, errors on duplicate labels, and has side effects). Works across markdown-family and Sweave/LaTeX/HTML patterns.
- Unlabeled chunks get an automatic label (`unnamed-chunk-N`); text and inline code between chunks are ignored.

## Tests

Added to `tests/testit/test-parser.R`:
- reads chunks from an `.Rmd` (label + multi-line body, options stripped)
- reads chunks from an `.Rnw`
- unlabeled document chunk gets an automatic label
- a `.R` script (even with a fence-like string in a comment) is still parsed as a script, not misdetected as a document

Regression suites (`parser`, `patterns`, `block`, `output`, `chunk`, `utils`, `tangle`) all pass.

## Note

As @atusy noted in the thread, reusing chunks across documents has caveats (hidden dependencies on variables/packages; harder to trace which file uses a chunk). This PR only adds the capability that was requested; it doesn't encourage it over factoring shared code into an R script/function.

title: Pass engine-modified chunk options to the chunk hook (#2333)
description:
Fixes #2333.

A language engine can modify the chunk options before producing output — e.g. set `options$results = 'asis'` and then call `engine_output()`. Those modified options were passed to the `output` hook (through `sew()`), but the `chunk` hook still received the options as **declared in the chunk header**. The two hooks could therefore disagree, which is what @cderv reported: Quarto redefines the `chunk` hook to wrap output and keys the wrapping on `options$results`, so an engine that sets `results = 'asis'` internally still got its output wrapped, even though the `output` hook already treated it as `asis`.

## Reproducer (from the issue)

An engine sets `results = 'asis'`; a user `chunk` hook wraps non-asis output in `::: {.wrapped}` and an `output` hook wraps non-asis output in `::: {.internal}`. Before this change, the demo chunk's output is still wrapped in `.wrapped` (chunk hook sees the header default) while `.internal` is correctly omitted (output hook sees the engine's change). After the change, both hooks agree and neither wraps the asis output.

## Change

- `engine_output()` attaches the (possibly engine-modified) `options` to its returned value as a `chunk_opts` attribute.
- `block_exec()` recovers those options after calling the engine, before running the `after` hooks and the `chunk` hook, so every hook sees the same options.

The recovery is guarded (`is.list(attr(output, 'chunk_opts'))`), so engines that don't go through `engine_output()` (e.g. plot engines returning image paths) are unaffected.

## Tests

Added a regression test in `tests/testit/test-engine.R`: an engine sets `results = 'asis'`, and the test asserts the `chunk` hook observes `options$results == 'asis'`. Verified it fails without the fix and passes with it.

title: purl(): resolve YAML params referenced in chunk options (#1938)
description:
Closes #1938.

## Problem

When `purl()`ing (tangling) an R Markdown document whose YAML front matter defines `params`, a chunk whose *options* reference those params was silently dropped from the tangled script:

````
---
params:
  paramcd: TRUE
---

```{r, eval = params$paramcd}
print(params$paramcd)
```
````

`knitr::purl(text = ...)` produced a script containing only `params <- list(paramcd = TRUE)` — the code chunk was gone. `tangle_block()` evaluates `eval`/`purl`/`child` options via `eval_lang()`; because `params` was not defined in `knit_global()` at tangle time, the evaluation errored, which is treated as "cannot determine the option → do not purl", so the chunk was excluded.

## Fix

When tangling, assign the flattened YAML `params` list into `knit_global()` (in `knit()` in `R/output.R`, where the params block is already computed for the tangled output). `eval_lang()` can then resolve `params$...` in chunk options. Parsing the YAML `params` field does not involve evaluating any document code, so tangling remains a purely static operation (per the discussion in the issue).

## Result

- `eval = params$foo` → chunk kept; if it resolves to `FALSE`, the code is commented out (as with a literal `eval = FALSE`).
- `purl = params$foo` → honored (chunk dropped when `FALSE`).
- Documents without YAML `params` are unaffected.

Added tests in `tests/testit/test-tangle.R` and a NEWS entry.

title: sql engine: add sql.result.fun to customize result production (#1778)
description:
Closes #1778.

Adds an opt-in chunk option **`sql.result.fun`**, a `function(conn, query)` that produces the chunk's result object in place of the built-in DBI execution. This lets a `sql` chunk return an object that should **not** be collected eagerly — the use case from the issue: a lazy table for downstream **dplyr** composition.

````
```{r}
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
lazy <- function(conn, query) dplyr::tbl(conn, dbplyr::sql(query))
```

```{sql, connection=con, output.var="q1", sql.result.fun=lazy}
SELECT mpg, cyl FROM mtcars
```

```{r}
q1 %>% filter(cyl == 4) %>% summarise(avg = mean(mpg))  # composed lazily, collected here
```
````

`q1` is a `tbl_lazy` — the query is not executed until `collect()` (or a print) is triggered downstream.

## How it works

- `run_query()` delegates to `sql.result.fun(conn, query)` when the option is set, instead of calling `DBI::dbExecute`/`dbGetQuery`. The function decides whether/how to touch the database.
- With `output.var`, the returned object is assigned to that variable and nothing is collected.
- Without `output.var`, `render_output()` prints the object using its own method (e.g. the lazy-table preview) rather than coercing it through `kable()`/`head()`, which would force collection.
- A non-function value raises an informative error.

The chunk still gets the `sql` engine's syntax highlighting and option handling, which was the motivation for wanting this inside `eng_sql` rather than a bare custom engine.

## Tests

Added a test (guarded on `RSQLite`) that a custom `sql.result.fun` is used in place of DBI execution: the query is passed through without being run, assigned to `output.var`, and a non-function value is rejected.

title: sql engine: add sql.interlaced for multi-statement output (#2093)
description:
Addresses #2093.

A multi-statement `sql` chunk previously submitted the whole block in a single DBI call. Depending on the backend, statements after the first could be silently dropped (e.g. RSQLite warns `Ignoring remaining part of query`), and only one result was rendered.

## What this adds

A new opt-in chunk option **`sql.interlaced`**. When `TRUE`, the chunk is split into individual statements, each is executed in order, and the source + result of each are emitted as an alternating (interlaced) sequence of blocks — like an R chunk echoing each expression with its result.

````
```{sql, connection=con, sql.interlaced=TRUE}
SELECT 1 AS A;
SELECT 2 AS A, 'B' AS B
```
````

renders as:

```` markdown
``` sql
SELECT 1 AS A
```
| A |
|--:|
| 1 |

``` sql
SELECT 2 AS A, 'B' AS B
```
| A | B |
|--:|:--|
| 2 | B |
````

The default (no option) behavior is unchanged.

## Statement splitting

Per the discussion, splitting is done by a new **pure-R** helper `split_sql()` — no Python/`sqlparse` dependency. It scans the code and only splits on top-level semicolons, ignoring semicolons inside:

- string literals (`'...'`, including `'''` escapes)
- quoted identifiers (`"..."` and `` `...` ``)
- comments (`-- ...`, `# ...`, and `/* ... */`)

It tokenizes only enough to find statement boundaries; it does not validate SQL.

## Behavior details

- The single-statement path is refactored into `run_query()` / `render_output()` helpers and is behavior-compatible with before (existing `test-sql.R` passes unchanged).
- In interlaced mode, execution stops at the first failing statement (respecting the `error` chunk option).
- `output.var` in interlaced mode captures the list of results from all executed statements.

## Tests

Added `split_sql()` unit tests (strings, escapes, quoted identifiers, all comment styles) and, guarded on `RSQLite` availability, integration tests for interlaced rendering, error stopping, single-statement equivalence, and `output.var` capture.

title: Expand chunk references embedded in a line (#2034)
description:
Closes #2034.

## Problem

A chunk reference like `<<label>>` is only recognized when it sits alone on its own line, because the `ref.chunk` pattern is anchored:

```r
'^\\s*<<(.+)>>\\s*$'
```

So in the reporter's example, the last reference (alone on its line) expands, but the earlier one with a trailing pipe does not:

````
```{r, eval=FALSE}
mtcars %>%
  <<filterCyl>> %>%   # NOT expanded — trailing `%>%` breaks the anchor
  <<filterGear>>      # expanded
```
````

## Fix

`parse_chunk()` gains a second pass (`fill_inline_ref()`) that expands references appearing anywhere in a line, not just on a line of their own:

- The line is split into alternating literal-text and reference segments.
- `paste_lines()` concatenates the segments "horizontally": the last line of one segment is joined with the first line of the next.
- A referenced chunk that spans **multiple lines** is spliced into the line; continuation lines are indented to the leading whitespace of the host line. A trailing reference (the common case, e.g. `x %>% <<foo>>`) expands cleanly across lines.
- Unknown labels are left verbatim.

The existing whole-line pass — which preserves the indentation of multi-line insertions — is unchanged.

After the fix the reporter's example renders as:

```r
mtcars %>%
  dplyr::filter(cyl == 6L) %>%
  dplyr::filter(gear == 4L)
```

And a multi-line chunk splices in place:

````
```{r multi, eval=FALSE}
group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(n = n())
```
```{r, eval=FALSE}
mtcars %>%
  <<multi>>
```
````
→
```r
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(n = n())
```

## Tests

Added cases to `tests/testit/test-parser.R`:
- reference embedded in a line with a trailing operator
- multiple references on one line
- unknown labels left untouched
- multi-line chunk spliced into a line, with continuation lines indented to the host line

Regression suites (`parser`, `patterns`, `block`, `output`, `chunk`, `utils`) all pass.

title: R latex pattern
description:
This pull request adds a new pattern for defining R code chunks within a LaTeX environment, replacing the <<>>= ... @ syntax.
```
\begin{Rcode}[options]
## code goes here
\end{Rcode}
```
The pattern is associated with files with an .RLatex extension. Ideally, I would like this syntax to be just another option for .Rnw files, but for now, I think this approach is less likely to create conflicts with existing code.

Why did I do this? My development environment is emacs/ESS, and when writing ordinary LaTeX documents, I use the preview-latex emacs package to preview LaTeX math inline. However, preview-latex chokes on R code chunks, and I have not found a way to tell it to skip everything between <<>>= and @. But I can tell preview-latex to skip an environment. So preview-latex thinks the code chunk is just an environment to skip, and knitr knows that the Rcode environment contains code to be knitted. Everyone is happy.

I created a gist that goes into more detail, with examples (including some additions to the LaTeX preamble). The gist also contains a new polymode, so ESS can recognize the contents of the Rcode environment as code, and execute syntax highlighting, indentation, etc., appropriately. That's not part of knitr, but I mention it here for those who are interested.

Of course, I could just define the pattern in a hook to run whenever knitr loads. But that would make my documents non-portable. So I am hoping this contribution is worthy of addition to the package, and that others can benefit.

title: tikz engine: add engine.opts$density to control raster resolution (#2114)
description:
Closes #2114.

When the `tikz` engine converts the compiled PDF to a bitmap format (e.g. PNG), the resolution is determined by the density at which **magick** reads the PDF (`magick::image_read_pdf(density=)`). This was previously fixed at the magick default of 300 DPI with no way to change it.

The behavior documented in older NEWS (setting `-density 300` via `convert.opts`) has not worked since v1.22, when the tikz engine switched from the command-line ImageMagick `convert` tool to the **magick** package. Passing `convert.opts = '-density 300'` now actually errors, because it is spliced into `magick::image_convert()` (which has no `density` argument):

```

```

This PR adds an `engine.opts$density` element (defaulting to `300` to preserve current output) that is passed to `image_read_pdf()`, so users can request higher-resolution tikz output:

````
```{tikz, engine.opts = list(density = 600)}

\node (a) {A};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

title: Separate subfigures with \\ instead of \newline for correct centering
description:
Fixes #1907.

When subfigures (`fig.subcap`) span multiple rows, knitr separated the rows with `\newline`. Using `\\` ends the line while respecting the alignment, so the subfigures are centered as expected. `\\` also respects left/right alignment, so other alignments are unaffected.

This matches the diagnosis in the issue thread (and [this TeX SE answer](https://tex.stackexchange.com/questions/457917/subfloat-vertical-alignment)).

Verified end-to-end by compiling the reporter's example to PDF: with `\newline` the subfigures render left-aligned; with `\\` they render centered.

title: Use the first device (with its dev.args) as the recording device
description:
Fixes #1323.

When multiple graphics devices are requested, e.g.

```r
dev = c('cairo_pdf', 'svglite'),
dev.args = list(cairo_pdf = list(pointsize = 8), svglite = list(pointsize = 8))
```

`chunk_device()` only opens a single recording device. It had per-device openers (with the matching `dev.args`) for the single-device case only, so with a device *vector* it fell through to the default `pdf` device with default arguments. Since the recording device's `pointsize` affects the final output regardless of each output device's own `pointsize` (#1235), the recorded plot ended up with the wrong `pointsize`.

This records with the **first** device in the list and its `dev.args`, so measurement-affecting arguments take effect. Output devices are unaffected — each is still replayed with its own `dev.args` in `plot2dev()`. Single-device behavior is unchanged.

Regression test in `tests/testit/test-plot.R` checks that `dev = c('png', 'pdf')` opens `png` (not the fallback `pdf`) as the recording device.

title: Support fig.topcaption for LaTeX output
description:
Fixes #1990.

The chunk option `fig.topcaption` places a figure's caption above the figure instead of below it. It was only wired into the HTML markdown hook (`hook_plot_md`); for LaTeX/PDF output the caption was always emitted at the bottom of the figure environment.

In LaTeX the caption position is determined by where `\caption` appears relative to `\includegraphics`, so when `fig.topcaption` is `TRUE`, `hook_plot_tex()` now emits `\caption` right after `\begin{figure}` instead of before `\end{figure}`. The figure note (`fig.note`) still goes at the bottom, and the default (bottom-caption) output is unchanged.

Regression test in `tests/testit/test-hooks-latex.R` checks the caption/image order for both settings, that the caption stays inside the figure environment, and that it is emitted only once.

title: Detect read_chunk() calls in purl() by parsing code, not string matching
description:
Fixes #1753.

`purl()` located `read_chunk()` calls with the regex `read_chunk\(([^)]+)\)`, treating the chunk as a string rather than code. As @rgayler diagnosed, that captured string is not guaranteed to be well-formed even when the chunk is. It:

- broke on a closing parenthesis inside a string argument (e.g. `read_chunk(lines = ")")`), crashing `purl()` with a parse error;
- matched functions merely ending in `read_chunk` (e.g. `fake_read_chunk()`);
- matched commented-out calls.

This parses the chunk and walks the syntax tree instead, evaluating only genuine `read_chunk()` calls — including namespaced `knitr::read_chunk()`. Parsing drops comments and handles nested parentheses and strings natively (the "wrong closing parenthesis" case @yihui noted regex can't solve).

Regression tests in `tests/testit/test-tangle.R` cover the reprex from the issue (no crash) and a genuine `read_chunk()` pulling in external code.

title: current_input() returns the original .qmd name under Quarto (#2384)
description:
Fixes #2384.

When a `.qmd` document is rendered by Quarto, Quarto first generates an intermediate `.rmarkdown` file and passes *that* to knitr. As a result, `knitr::current_input()` returned e.g. `"doc.rmarkdown"` instead of the `"doc.qmd"` that users expect (see the discussion in #2384, where this was confirmed surprising).

This maps the input name back to `.qmd` in `current_input()` when knitr detects it is running under Quarto (the `quarto.version` knit option is set). Only the reported name changes; the internal `infile` (used for line numbers, concordance, etc.) is left untouched, since the `.rmarkdown` file is the one actually knitted.

```r
# under Quarto, infile = "doc.rmarkdown"
current_input()       # -> "doc.qmd"   (was "doc.rmarkdown")
```

Tests added in `test-utils.R` cover the Quarto case, the non-Quarto case (name reported as-is), and that other extensions are untouched.

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

title: Add `knit_cnd_format()` generic
description:
rlang is now in charge of fully printing error messages, including the error prefix. This makes it possible to support more features, such as custom display of condition calls and chained errors.

```r
mtcars |> dplyr::summarise(cyl = 1 + "")
#> Error in `dplyr::summarise()`:
#>   Problem while computing `cyl = 1 + ""`.
#> Caused by error in `+`:
#>   non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

Ideally, the condition messages in knitted documents should match the messages in the REPL. This is currently achieved for errors via an `as.character.rlang_error()` method that is called by `sew.error()`. However, methods for other conditions do not call `as.character()`. Also that customisation point is not very explicit and is probably to be considered off-label usage from the point of view of knitr.

To solve these issues, this PR proposes to add a new generic for the full formatting of condition messages, including the prefix. Example usage can be found in https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/pull/1323/files.

cc @hadley

title: Spin comments
description:
These examples are the same as in \#1801. With this PR an error is thrown

skimming txt2 I would ex the first “comment” block to be in the .Rmd file,
the R code chunk to be omitted, the statment “annother comment” to be in the
.Rmd, and last line to be omitted. This is assuming that an error isn’t

I included a line in `NEWS.md` describing this. However, I did not include a test. title: added "rmarkdown" engine to process code blocks
description:
I ran into a situation where I wanted to be able to turn on or off different pieces of commentary in the markdown throughout a document. For example, I would ideally like to set a flag to include more technical commentary for an analytic audience, but then strip them out for a general audience.  

Although the `asis` engine works in most cases, it doesn't process inline code blocks that I often use for communicating results. To address this, I added a new `rmarkdown` engine to pre-process the text using `knitr::knit`.

Here is an example document where this is useful:

`````
---
title: "test"
output: pdf_document
---

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# create a flag to easily turn on/off markdown 'code' blocks
.show_analysis_commentary <- TRUE
```

this is some general text

```{r analysis, echo = FALSE}
# derive answer to life, the universe and everything
var <- 42
```

```{rmarkdown, echo = .show_analysis_commentary}
# print out analysis result only if `.show_analysis_commentary` is `TRUE`
the answer to life, the universe and everything is `r sprintf('%.f', var)`
```

```{r}
hist(mtcars$mpg)
```
`````

---
_let me know if any tests should be added. I couldn't find any for the `asis` engine and figured this would only necessitate a similar level of testing._

title: fix: apply the ditaa engine's default arguments
description:
`R/engine.R:423` supplies ditaa's default arguments behind `if (cmd == 'ditta')`. `cmd` is `options$engine` and the registered engine is `ditaa`, so the branch can never be taken. Three lines below, the same `cmd` in the same list is spelled correctly.

The miss is silent: the `if` has no `else` and returns `NULL` invisibly, `list_fun()` wraps it as `function() NULL`, and `c(opts$args1(), ...)` at `:210` concatenates nothing. So every ditaa chunk has run with ditaa's stock settings since the arguments were added in #2092, and the comment on the line above has promised otherwise since 2022.

```
before   running: ditaa                   in.ditaa in.ditaa
after    running: ditaa -s 2 -T -S -E     in.ditaa in.ditaa
```

**This changes rendered output for existing ditaa users**: `-s 2` scales 2x, `-T` makes the background transparent, `-S` drops shadows, `-E` disables edge separation. That is your stated intent on the line above, but it is visible, so if you would rather keep the current effective behaviour and delete the dead line instead, say so and I will close this.

<details>
<summary>Verification</summary>

R 4.6.1, `testit`, full `tests/run-all.R` with `R CMD INSTALL` before every row.

| row | `R/engine.R` md5 | exit | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| master + the new test | `9ca8d174f2b0d41c17f4fa4fb677b6e9` | 1 | fails assertion 1: `grepl("^ditaa -s 2 -T -S -E ", ...)` is FALSE |
| this change | `4fb08ef30025b29a7d56f66cbbed431f` | **0** | whole suite OK |
| drop the condition entirely | `4261d31af7d2f06f48e48d120a182c70` | 1 | fails assertion 2, on **both** `dot` and `asy` |

The two mutants kill different assertions, so neither test case is redundant: the first proves the ditaa row, the second proves that `dot` and `asy` must not inherit the arguments.

The test captures the `running: ...` message `eng_exec` emits before `system2`, so **it needs no `ditaa`, `dot` or `asy` binary** and is safe on every CI leg.

I checked the other key lookups in `R/` for the same shape: `R/engine.R:427-428` covers all three registered engines, `R/block.R:531` is restricted by `match.arg`, and both `R/table.R` alignment lookups are guarded at `:220`. This is the only one with no producer.

No roxygen comment is touched, so no `man/` regeneration.

title: Unwrap Pandoc raw ```{=typst} blocks in Typst output (#2462)
description:
Fixes #2462.

## Problem

`results = "asis"` appeared broken for `.Rtyp` (RTypst) documents: output from `knit_print()` methods that produce Typst tables was shown as a literal code block instead of being rendered.

The root cause is that such methods (e.g. `typstable`'s `knit_print.typst_table`, or anything using `knitr::raw_block(x, "typst")`) wrap their output in a **Pandoc raw block**:

````
```{=typst}
#table(...)
```
````

This is the correct convention when the `.typ` is post-processed by Pandoc (Quarto/R Markdown), where Pandoc strips the fence and injects raw Typst. But `knit2pdf('input.Rtyp')` compiles the `.typ` **directly with the `typst` binary** — no Pandoc — so the fence survives and Typst renders it as a literal code block.

## Fix

Add a `document` output hook to `hooks_typst()` that unwraps Pandoc raw ```` ```{=typst} ```` blocks to their raw content. Other fenced code blocks (e.g. ```` ```rust ````) are left untouched.

## Test

Added `tests/testit/test-hooks-typst.R` covering unwrapping, multiple blocks, and preservation of unrelated code fences. Full `testit` suite passes (`test-plot.R` fails only due to a local "Graphics API version mismatch" unrelated to this change).
